To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The average lapse time between the end the teacher’s question (or statement) and the beginning of student response is 2.5 seconds.

the lapse time between the teacher’s question (Q) and the student’s response (R) is a function of both Q and R, that the relationship between the levels of Q and R is a strong one, but that lapse times do not increase directly as Q or R levels increase.

(1) the lapse time between a teacher’s question and a student’s response increases with the hierarchal level of the question, (2) the lapse time increases with the hierachial level of the response, and (3) the lapse time is longer when the student responds at a higher level than the question level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether or not teachers are asking higher order questions of students and, if so, whether students respond to such questions in higher order thinking.
the question of the relationship between the cognitive functioning of the teacher and his students as reflected in the levels of their respective questions and responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the level of question asked and the level of response received are both related to lapse time, but that this relationship is not direct.
lapse time increases directly with the level of the question and with the level of responding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the elementary school child, the teacher’s question level has a direct effect on the child’s level of responding, but that the teacher’s question has no direct effect on the lapse time between question and response.
the level of the question asked by the elementary teacher is an important variable in determining student response level and lapse time.
teachers should be encouraged to ask questions that require higher levels of cognitive functioning from their students.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the teacher’s use of higher level questions does not automatically lead the student to higher level responses.
the teacher should not expect a student to respond at a level higher than the level at which he is asked the question.
